title: Hubble sees stars as numerous as grains of sand in nearby galaxy
caption: Stars in the heart of spiral galaxy NGC 300, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IRAS 00525-3757, NGC 300 · constellation Sculptor · about 7 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, and The Hubble Heritage Team (AURA/STScI)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: Countless stars fill this Hubble image of the heart of NGC 300, each resolved as its own point of light like grains of sand on a beach. Hot, young blue stars cluster in the spiral arms, ribbons of deep red trace curtains of dust that partly hide the stars behind, and near the center lies the galaxy's bright, compact nucleus.

NGC 300 is a spiral much like the Milky Way and one of its closer neighbors, 6.5 million light-years away in the Sculptor group. From the ground only its brightest stars can be singled out, but Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with resolution some 10 times sharper, separates many more. Even so, the packed nucleus defeats it.

These data are testing a new way to measure distances to galaxies, using luminous blue supergiants. By combining their brightness with temperature, surface gravity and mass outflow, astronomers hope to check it against traditional methods based on Cepheid variables.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.95 x 4.66 arcminutes) and distance (7 million light years), the frame spans roughly 6,000 × 9,500 light-years. Its light set out about 7 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This color composite was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys from images taken through blue, green and near-infrared filters. The exact color assigned to each filter is not published.
understand.eye: Part of the light is near-infrared, invisible to the eye, and no eye or ground-based telescope could separate these stars as Hubble does.

explore: The Sculptor group of galaxies is named for the southern constellation in which it is found.
Measuring distances is a perpetual but important concern in astronomy, and Cepheids, stars that pulsate with a period linked to their brightness, have long been one of the standard tools.
alt: A dense field of individual stars with clusters of blue stars, reddish dust ribbons and a bright compact nucleus near the center.
